clue.text: Musically, they get heated around noon — and Mendelssohn gig could be the reason!

parts.note: being crazy could be the reason anyone goes out in the midday heat, so this phrase supplies MAD

indicators.note: set to music, the letters of the phrase that follows are played in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, the fodder to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A musical joke: a Mendelssohn concert might be why people overheat at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musically' rearranges AND MENDELSSOHN GIG to DOGS AND ENGLISHMEN, and 'could be the reason' supplies MAD, the craziness behind it. Noel Coward's song says they go out in the midday sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel Coward's song says these people go out in the midday sun, so they are the ones getting hot at noon.

clue.text: Over and over again I confirm my occupation as seamstress

indicators.note: turning over reverses the order of the letters
doing it over again means the short phrase appears twice

parts.note: 'I'm' declares occupation of a place, short for I am

explanation.surface: A worker repeatedly states what her job is: she sews.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over again' doubles IM to IMIM and 'Over' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Puccini's opera La Boheme is a poor embroiderer of flowers.

clue.text: Degas, at his peak The Greatest Artist

indicators.note: the top letter of the painter's name, in a down light

parts.note: Muhammad Ali called himself The Greatest

explanation.surface: Degas in his prime was the greatest painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artist' is the definition, not Degas.
explanation.definitionFit: Salvador Dali was the Spanish surrealist painter.

clue.text: All dead fruit, I presume

parts.note: read backwards from the answer, zero lives remaining is everyone dead

explanation.surface: Someone presumes all the fruit has gone bad.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: split the answer as O LIVES, 'nought lives', and it describes 'All dead'. 'I presume' signals the guess.
explanation.definitionFit: Olives are the small stone fruits of the Mediterranean tree.

clue.text: Nick's missus has climax frequently, it's said — and guess who's here!

indicators.note: the wife holds the other parts, so they go inside her

parts.note: Old Nick is the devil, so his wife would be a she-devil
a peak is a high point
oft is an old word for often

explanation.surface: Gossip about a woman's love life is interrupted when she walks in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's said' is not a sound signal; it introduces the saying.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb is said when someone being discussed turns up unexpectedly.

clue.text: Keen, like pretty maids in garden, heading off to secure a little rumpy-pumpy

indicators.note: the trimmed phrase holds the extra letter inside it
the leading letter is taken away

parts.note: the nursery rhyme Mary Mary Quite Contrary ends 'pretty maids all in a row'

indicators.note: only a small portion, the first letter, of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A garden scene from the nursery rhyme turns into some saucy goings-on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' leaves NAROW, and 'to secure' puts R, from 'a little rumpy-pumpy', inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A keen or narrow margin is a fine one; Chambers lists the two as synonyms.

clue.text: Second crew's existence doubly confirmed

indicators.note: saying the same thing twice confirms it, so the piece for existence is written two times

parts.note: existence is what is, so 'is' stands for it

explanation.surface: A rowing club's reserve boat has its existence double-checked.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isis is the name of the Thames at Oxford, and Oxford's reserve Boat Race crew is called Isis.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford University's reserve rowing eight, behind the Blue Boat, races under this name.

clue.text: So UK (or US — OK?), he eats out — here?

definitions.text: So UK (or US — OK?), he eats out — here?

indicators.note: out signals the letters are scrambled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Whether in Britain or America, a man goes out for a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'or US — OK?' is a joke version of SO UK in the transatlantic spelling and is not fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A grill restaurant is a place where a man in Britain or America eats out.

clue.text: 'The City of London' = cunning 'undercover' movement I infiltrated …

indicators.note: the movement and the I creep inside the other letters
a cunning plan twists things, so the sign's word is rearranged

parts.note: the sign reads as 'equals'
REM, rapid eye movement, happens under the bedcovers in sleep

explanation.surface: A spy ring has secretly infiltrated the financial district.
explanation.walkthrough: The = sign is read as a word, then 'cunning' rearranges it. REM is rapid eye movement, which happens under the bedcovers in sleep; 'infiltrated' puts it and I inside.
explanation.definitionFit: London's financial district occupies roughly one square mile, the nickname.

clue.text: One induced a little man to wear hats out east

indicators.note: the man is put on by the hats, so his letters go inside them
the compass point is taken out of the headgear word

parts.note: millinery is the trade and stock of women's hats
E is the compass abbreviation for east
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: Someone persuaded a small fellow to try on some hats in the east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One induced a little' is the definition: a small unit of electrical inductance, not a persuaded person.
explanation.definitionFit: A thousandth of a henry, the SI unit of inductance, is a small amount of induction.

clue.text: The fop Burlington Bertie's home, I've heard

indicators.note: the speaker reports what was heard, so the place name is taken by its sound

parts.note: the music-hall song is 'Burlington Bertie from Bow', Bow being a district of East London

explanation.surface: A dandy is said to live where the music-hall toff Burlington Bertie came from.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is a district of East London; the song 'Burlington Bertie from Bow' is about a penniless would-be toff.
explanation.definitionFit: A beau is an old word for a dandy, a man fussy about his clothes.

clue.text: …blame me for extra clause adopting unusual angle

parts.note: a rider is an added clause to a document

indicators.note: made unusual, the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Continuing from 8 down, the spy chief accepts blame for a strange extra clause.
explanation.definitionFit: The leader of a group of wrongdoers is the one who takes the blame.

clue.text: Bishop on top of daughter in the trees? Rubbish

indicators.note: in a down light the bishop sits above the rest

parts.note: B is the chess notation for bishop

indicators.note: the daughter goes between the two trees

parts.note: the alder is a tree
the ash is a tree

explanation.surface: A churchman perched above a girl up a tree: nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean nonsense or worthless talk.

clue.text: My boss backing some literary satire, I left work saved here?

indicators.note: going backwards, the boss's letters are read in reverse

parts.note: a crossword setter's boss is the editor, ED

indicators.note: the I has left, so it is removed from the satire word

parts.note: a skit is a short satirical piece
OP, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: An office worker quits after their boss reverses a satirical piece, wondering where the work was saved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns ED to DE; 'left' drops the I from SKIT. 'here?' asks where computer files are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Files are often saved to the computer screen's main area, the virtual work surface.

clue.text: Sign on cap of clot I am with — it's his like

parts.note: a dunce's cap is marked with a D
I'm is short for I am
taken without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone stands beside a fool and admits they are alike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'his like' means people like the clot.
explanation.definitionFit: A clot is a stupid person, and people of his kind are stupid people too.

clue.text: Greek airline once entertained all the characters here

parts.note: Pan Am was a famous US airline that ceased flying in 1991

explanation.definitionFit: A sentence using every letter of the alphabet is one where all the characters appear.

clue.text: I take and answer first part of exam — 'Southern Nationals'

parts.note: R stands for recipe, Latin for 'take', on prescriptions
Q1, question one, is the first part of an exam paper

explanation.surface: A candidate answers the opening question of a paper set by Southern examiners.
explanation.walkthrough: R for 'take' comes from the Latin 'recipe' heading old prescriptions.

clue.text: Pedestrian member of Mainwaring's platoon

definitions.meaning: Private ..., the spiv in the BBC sitcom Dad's Army, led by Captain Mainwaring

explanation.definitionFit: A pedestrian is someone on foot, and Private Joe Walker was the spiv in Dad's Army, a classic BBC sitcom.

clue.text: Elderly person has initially accessed it through rigged swing door?

definitions.text: Elderly person has initially accessed it through rigged swing door?

indicators.note: the elderly person holds everything else, his letters standing at both ends

parts.note: GOM, Grand Old Man, an elderly figure

indicators.note: the letters go through the door, so they sit inside it
a rigged door has been tampered with, so its letters are rearranged
only the opening letter of the following word is taken

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An old man has got in through a fiddled swing door.
explanation.walkthrough: GOM, Grand Old Man, wraps the rest. 'rigged' rearranges SWING DOOR to DSWINGROO, and 'through' puts A (first of 'accessed') plus IT inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A jokey name for a seaside town full of retired people, where the old seem to wait for the end.

clue.text: Entry above these birds would provide way out

definitions.text: Entry above these birds would provide way out

parts.words: Entry above these birds would provide way out
parts.note: in a dictionary the headword just before these herons is EGRESS, an exit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Entry' is a dictionary headword, not a doorway: the word listed just above is EGRESS, which means a way out.
explanation.definitionFit: Small white herons are the birds, and the word above them in a dictionary means an exit.

clue.text: Hot German bread with the middle cut out

parts.note: stollen is a German fruit loaf eaten at Christmas

explanation.surface: A spicy German loaf with its centre sliced away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot' is the definition in its slang sense, not a temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot goods are ones that have been pinched; the slang sense of theft.

clue.text: The poor little boy of Jonathan Selby

explanation.definitionFit: In the Grimm tale the poor woodcutter's son is abandoned in the forest with his sister Gretel.

clue.text: Admit us if rowdy? Probably not

definitions.text: Admit us if rowdy? Probably not

clue.text: One given to eat sandwiches then rolls (mutton)

indicators.note: rolling over turns the assembled letters end to end
the food word is placed either side of the single letter, like bread round a filling

parts.note: fed means given food to eat
A means one

explanation.walkthrough: 'sandwiches' puts A inside FED, giving FAED, and 'rolls' turns it round. 'Mutton' is rhyming slang: Mutt and Jeff, cartoon characters, rhymes with the answer.

clue.text: Resolute business organisation

clue.text: Jockey's unseated at start of 4 o'clock in German urban area

explanation.definitionFit: Germany's Ruhr is a large industrial conurbation of cities such as Essen and Dortmund.
